vignette:
He is 74 now, a South Eastern Asian man with large, careful hands that still bear the small burns and silver scars of a lifetime spent welding. He speaks quietly, often looking down before he answers, as if he has first to pass through a place inside himself that is crowded and loud. He has been married for decades. His wife, he says, is patient, though he knows she has lived for years with a man who never fully came home.

When he is a young man, war comes to his town and turns ordinary life into something watchful and unstable. At first he tells himself he can adjust. People still need roofs repaired, gates fixed, engines patched. Metal still breaks and must be mended, so he keeps working where he can, carrying tools from one damaged building to another. He learns to notice the difference between distant gunfire and shelling that is coming closer. He learns how quickly a marketplace can empty. He learns that the air before an explosion has its own kind of silence.

The moment he returns to most often is not one grand battle scene but a day that begins like many others. He is moving between streets with two other men, hoping to reach a workshop where they have heard there is work. He remembers the heat, the smell of dust and diesel, and then the sudden blast that throws him down. For a few seconds he cannot understand what has happened. His ears ring so sharply that the world seems to vanish. When the sound returns, it comes back as screaming. One of the men beside him is badly wounded. Another does not move. He remembers seeing pieces of brick, a sandal in the road, smoke rising from a place that had held people just moments before. He tries to help, but there is blood everywhere, and the next explosion comes before he can think clearly. Afterward, he says, something in him no longer believes that any place is safe.

He survives the war, marries, works, and eventually builds a life that from the outside looks solid. Welding suits him. It is exacting work, and he trusts metal more than he trusts the world. He likes the clear tasks, the visible seams, the satisfaction of making something hold. But even in the workshop, he startles when a sheet of steel drops or a torch ignites with a sudden pop. The bright white arc sometimes pulls him backward without warning, and for an instant the sparks are not sparks but fragments from an explosion. He becomes known as a serious man, disciplined and hardworking, but also one who keeps to himself. He does not join coworkers when they linger to talk. He prefers to face the door. He checks exits automatically in every room.

At home, his wife learns not to wake him suddenly. In sleep he kicks, shouts, and once strikes the wall hard enough to bruise his hand. Some nights he wakes already sitting up, heart pounding, convinced he has heard shelling. He goes to the window before he is fully awake. Even after he realizes where he is, he cannot settle again for hours. The next day he is irritable and ashamed. He says very little about the dreams, only that they are “old scenes” that return as if they are happening now.

Over the years he tries to manage by narrowing his life. He avoids crowded markets, holiday fireworks, political news, and any film that contains war. He tells his family he is tired or busy, but his children have noticed for years that he grows tense in traffic, especially if there are sirens, shouting, or the backfire of a motorbike. If he is outside when he hears a loud bang, his whole body reacts before his mind catches up; he ducks, scans, and feels a rush of fear so strong that he cannot hear what anyone is saying to him. Later he is embarrassed by how exposed he feels. He covers this with anger, snapping at the people closest to him, then sitting alone with the guilt.

What troubles him most now is that age has not softened these memories. Retirement has given him more unstructured time, and the past fills it. When his hands are idle, his mind drifts back to the street, the smoke, the unmoving body of the man beside him. He wonders why he lived when others did not. He has never said this plainly to his family, but it sits heavily in him. His wife says he is physically present yet far away. He agrees. Even during family meals, a sudden sound can pull him out of the room inside himself. He watches his grandchildren play and feels both love and grief at once—love for their safety, grief for the years he spent braced against danger, unable to trust peace when it finally came.
